chapter_theme: Akananuru 321 to 340 (Nithilakkovai): men on the wealth road arguing with their hearts by the desert's robbers and dying travellers, wives waiting through the promised rains, night trysts at the elephant's plantain slope, courtesans boasting by Chola victories and a mother following an eloped daughter in thought; the fame of Thithiyan, Pazhaiyan, Thiraiyan, Athiyan and the three crowned houses measures private feeling.

321.reading: After the girl has eloped, her foster mother pictures the summer road of dry springs, a stag calling its doe to food, cowherds' muddy wells where elephants come with their calf, and asks whether the girl will rest in some hamlet shelter with her companion or walk on into the night with the bold youth, since she slipped off her pebble-filled anklets so her mother would not hear and crossed the bamboo hills.
321.nuance: Taking off the anklets (சிலம்பு கழீஇ) is done so their sound will not betray her, but it is also the act that marks a girl's passage to marriage; here she performs it herself, in secret, so the sign of the wedding and the sign of the flight are one act.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl has left home with a young man across the hills

comparisons.tenor: the clear call of the summer wind over the dry spring
the sound echoing in the clefts of the rock

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks her grief aloud

iraicchi.act: the stag leaves the iluppai flowers uneaten and calls in a male voice for his doe to come and feed
iraicchi.sense: the creatures of the road she took show a male who feeds his mate before himself, so the mother's fear holds a hope that the youth will so tend the girl

322.reading: Turning back at midnight in a storm from a tryst whose signal proved false, the man asks his heart whether it will languish alone, trembling like one falling from a broken cliff, and says the girl who torments him is as hard to win as Thithiyan's Pothiyil, whose honey-hung peak no climber can finish.
322.nuance: The simile turns puram fame to akam use: Thithiyan's war elephants and spears are named before his hill, so Pothiyil is hard to enter not only for its steepness but because a fierce lord guards it, as her people guard her.

colophon.thurai: அல்லகுறிப்பட்டுப் போகின்ற தலைமகன் தன் னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover at midnight who cannot reach the girl

comparisons.tenor: the heart trembling with unsated desire
the heart left alone through the night
the girl, hard to obtain

323.reading: The friend bids the heroine, whom she hails as one who excels in wifely virtue, to step out gently on her small feet and see: the cloud, dark as her hair, has come down over the bamboo slopes with thunder and hail like a moving herd of elephants, so the town's gossip will wither and the word that her lover will come will prove true.
323.nuance: The friend reads the rain as proof because the returning season was his pledge. The colophon files the poem under paalai, but its matter is waiting through the promised rains, which porul 1.6 gives to mullai.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits and the promised rains have broken

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds moving over the sky
the rain cloud, dark as her hair

324.reading: Reading their lord's mind after the campaign, his attendants say that his wife will now even have guests to feed, for his chariot is racing through the rain-fed forest, past brimming pools and flower-strewn sand, its wheels cutting tracks where the water runs like a snake, to reach town in the jasmine evening.
324.nuance: விருந்தும், 'guests too': with the husband away the house could not receive guests, so his homecoming restores her duty as host as well as her joy.

thinai_evidence.note: forest after the rains at jasmine evening

comparisons.vehicle: கிள்ளை இனிதின் எடுத்த வளராப் பிள்ளைத் தூவி
comparisons.tenor: the green crops grown by the long rains
each brimming pool
the black sand streaked by the water
the water rushing in the wheel tracks

thurai_akam.speaker: ilaiyar
thurai_akam.note: the speakers are the hero's attendants (உழையர்), speaking among themselves

325.reading: The heroine tells her friend that her lover, seeing their secret love become gossip and her mother on guard, promised to take her with him once a day of cool rain had tamed the desert and asked her to wait a few days; instead, hardening his heart for his venture, he went alone at evening through the elephant-haunted waste toward Paanan's land in the north, and she asks what blame can fall on the fate that brings her this pain.
325.nuance: The desert is measured by a fallen patron: the hill lost its waterfalls as Athiyan's great drum went dead after him. She lays the broken promise on fate (பால்), not on him.

colophon.thurai: 1கொண்டு நீங்கக் கருதி யொழிந்த தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he promised to take her and went alone

comparisons.tenor: the hill whose beauty of waterfalls has died away

326.reading: Refusing the husband entry, the friend praises the young woman he courts, with her freckled lips, wide cool eyes and small forehead, lovely as the paddy fields by the bannered gate, says she must go to the festival in her finery, and adds that her eyes never miss whoever looks at them, as the spear Pazhaiyan of Por raised never missed.
326.nuance: The praise is ironic: eyes that never miss make the husband a target, not a chooser. Who the குறுமகள் is turns on reading: most likely the rival, though the lines could praise the wife's own beauty as wasted on him.

thinai_evidence.note: paddy fields and the watered Kaveri country

comparisons.tenor: the young woman's beauty
her eyes, which never miss

327.reading: The man rebukes his heart, which has resolved to go for wealth: if it knows that joy and grief, union and parting come by turns like midday and night, why should it cross a desert of mirages, withered marul and crows tearing at corpses, where killers pity no one and grieve only when their arrow misses; and if it goes, will it ever think of him again?
327.nuance: The opening is a sage's premise, that joy and grief alternate, used not to counsel acceptance but to argue against the journey: if hardship comes anyway in its turn, there is no need to go seeking it for wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a man arguing with his heart against the journey for wealth

comparisons.tenor: joy and grief, union and parting, which come by turns
the striped slough of the snake

328.reading: Speaking to her friend while the lover stands unseen nearby, the heroine says that had they known the man who came through the midnight storm, treading on snakes, to embrace her would grow weary of her, they would have held his chest again and again and never let it go: the chest of the man of the hill where a tusker strokes his mate as she sleeps among the plantains after calving.
328.nuance: Spoken to be overheard, the regret is a warning: the lover learns that his nights are being read as waning love, and the elephant pair beside its new calf shows the settled life he should offer.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover who comes by night to embrace her

comparisons.tenor: the thunder over the hill

iraicchi.act: the tusker tenderly strokes his young mate as she sleeps after bearing her calf
iraicchi.sense: the man of that hill, overhearing, is shown a male who stays and tends the mother of his young, the married life the heroine's words press him toward

329.reading: Her eyes and forehead pale with longing, the heroine tells her friend that if her lover can bear to live apart while she suffers, she wonders whether he will really go, resting only briefly, along the dusty road where salt merchants' carts wear out their oxen and over the hills of dry springs where a tigress whelps and a cub bites the trunk of a thirsty elephant.
329.nuance: She voices no fear for him on that violent road, only the question whether he can bear to live apart: the danger is set down as the land's own law, and the doubt is about his heart.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது. பிரிவுணர்த்திய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: he has resolved to leave across the waste

330.reading: Pleading the lover's case, the friend tells the heroine how he picked backwater flowers, lingered in the seaside grove, played at sand dolls, delighted them and humbled himself, and now goes away dejected because they have not understood his pain; her own unruly heart ran after him to stop him, and she wonders if it reached him and was too shy to speak, while his chariot over the white dunes rises and vanishes like a fisherman's boat in the open sea.
330.nuance: The friend speaks of her own heart running after him, lending her longing to win the heroine's; the chariot sinking and rising among the dunes shows the lover already slipping out of reach.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: seaside grove, dunes, screwpine and fishermen

comparisons.vehicle: சிறுகுடிப் பரதவர் பெருங்கடன் மடுத்த கடுஞ்செலற் கொடுந்திமில்
comparisons.tenor: his chariot rising and vanishing among the dunes

occasion.words: தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது

331.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man who left is without love: he went past many hill hamlets where women in leaf skirts carry from street to street the white iluppai flowers a bear has left, and across a waste as cruel as the sword Thithiyan, generous host of bards, drew against the Velir.
331.nuance: Two kinds of giving frame her complaint: hill women live on what the bear leaves, and Thithiyan fills bards' hands in his daily court; the waste the lover crossed is likened to that same giver's sword, his other face.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the waste and left her

comparisons.tenor: the white iluppai flowers
the bear's brood spread over the ground
the empty waste he crossed

332.reading: Speaking so the lover outside can hear, the heroine tells her friend that the words she once said lovingly, that the man of the hill where a tusker kills a tiger and then sleeps beside his mate among plantains is a man of grace fit for her, have come true: his embrace, which leaves no room even for a bee, and his love are as on the first day.
332.nuance: Praise spoken for the lover's ears: the tusker that kills the tiger and then rests with his mate gives the hero both faces the heroine claims for him, protector and constant companion.

thinai_evidence.note: bamboo, elephant and tiger of the hill slope

comparisons.tenor: his garlanded chest, to those who desire it
his embrace and love now

iraicchi.act: the tusker kills the tiger that lay in wait, then goes slowly to embrace his mate and sleeps beside her
iraicchi.sense: the man of that hill is one who both guards and stays, the grace the heroine says she found in him

333.reading: Answering a friend who scolds her for wasting with pallor and blaming him, and who says he would hurry home if told of her grief, the heroine prays the friend's sweet words come true, but says that even if he stays beyond the hills where elephants lift their trunks like withered summer palms, her pallor would easily fade if only a messenger came while he finishes his work, bringing his eager wish to return.
333.nuance: She asks for less than his return, only a messenger: what wastes her is the silence, not the distance.

thinai_evidence.note: he is far beyond the hills on his venture

comparisons.tenor: the pallor spreading over her body
the herd of elephants raising their trunks to the sky

334.reading: His campaign done and tribute taken, the hero tells his charioteer that the rains have begun, falling in streams like tuskers' trunks, with hail like girls' play-beads, and bids him drive the four horses, swift as a line of swans, without slackening through the peacock-filled fields, so that he may see at once his wife's kohl eyes, thick hair and small forehead.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains begin over the forest fields

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the rain
the streams of rain falling to the ground
the dark clouds gathering
the hailstones
the four horses running yoked together

335.reading: The man grants his heart that even the most compassionate cannot give without wealth, but says the cracked, lonely summer waste, where a tusker breaks his tusk stripping marā bark to feed his mate, would not be hard for them if they went taking the bright-bangled girl, whose red mouth, sweeter than the young areca of Chezhiyan's walled old town, flows with nectar; and so he gives up going alone.
335.nuance: The opening concedes the moral case for wealth in a maxim's terms: giving (ஈதல்) needs means. The answer is not a counter-maxim but the elephant, which provides for its mate at her side. Most of the poem is a description of the areca palm by Madurai's walls; how it maps onto her mouth is my reading.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சினைக் கழறிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the cracked summer waste

comparisons.tenor: the crown of the areca palm
the sheath of the spathe
the new flower cluster
the flower cluster opening for the bees
the white flowers spread below
the hail-like young fruit
the sweetness of her red mouth

iraicchi.act: the tusker breaks his own tusk prising bark off the dry marā so that his mate may eat in the cruel summer
iraicchi.sense: the male provides for his mate at her side, at his own cost, so the man sees that providing need not mean leaving her

336.reading: The courtesan the lord now favours says, for the other mistress's companions to hear, that the women who came in his chariot mock her beauty, but they go about as if they mattered only because she stays away from the festival, as a mahout lives on only by the killer elephant's mercy; if she comes and the lord of the otter-haunted ford does not turn with her as the nerunji turns with the sun, may her bangles break as the Aryan army broke at Vallam.
336.nuance: She stakes her bangles in the form of a warrior's oath on a Chola victory; but the bangle that slips or breaks is the sign of a woman abandoned, so the boast carries a fear.

thinai_evidence.note: otter, vaalai fish, kaanji shade and the pond's ford

comparisons.vehicle: பாகன் நெடிதுயிர் வாழ்தல் காய்சினக் கொல்களிற்று யானை நல்கல் மாறே
comparisons.tenor: the rival women's going about as if they mattered
the lord turning with her
her bangles breaking

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: she speaks for the hearing of the companions of the mistress kept in the house (இற்பரத்தை)

iraicchi.act: the male otter rises to bring the day's food to his mate, who lies unfed and weary with her young
iraicchi.sense: in the lord's own town a male provides for a mate weak with young, which recalls the wife and child he owes, against which the courtesan's boast is made

337.reading: When his heart again presses him to go for wealth, the man reminds it how once, finding it no joy to stay apart from her, it said 'let wealth stay where it is' and came back alone through the burnt, rainless waste where fierce Mazhavar cut down a starving brahmin messenger in case he carried gold, left in disgust at his rags, and a jackal dragged his entrails into the kalli shade, all because it feared she would suffer when the cold north wind came with the rains.
337.nuance: The murdered messenger is the poem's argument: on the wealth road a man is killed for what he might carry and found to carry nothing. The colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the one who went, came back and is tempted again is the man.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்துப் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்துவந்த தலைமகள் பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot forest the rains have deserted

comparisons.tenor: her body
the low hills crossed by many paths

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan

occasion.words: பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: the colophon reads தலைமகள்; the poem's speaker is the man

338.reading: After a tryst that failed, the man tells his heart that even if he cannot have the embrace of the dark girl whose forehead smells of kaanthal on the slope of the Pandyan's sacred hill, may their love last like the Porai's Kolli and may messages to her never stop, more numerous than the waves at the Chola's busy port.
338.nuance: Each crowned house lends a measure: the Pandyan's hill for where she lives, the Chera's Kolli for how long love should last, the Chola's sea for how many messages; what he asks is modest, that love and messages last, not union.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal on the hill slope where she lives

comparisons.tenor: their love, which must not perish
the messages to her

occasion.words: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

339.reading: Setting out as the cold season comes, when wheel ruts run with water like a snake and pulse pods split like loosening fingers, the man tells his heart that, pulled by manly duty and held by love, he is like an ant on a firebrand burning at both ends, and wonders whether she will suffer, she whose bond with him is as life joined to the body, whose love is like living and whose parting is like death.
339.nuance: Both ends of the firebrand burn, so the middle is no refuge: duty and love are equally fire. The closing triad gathers in three similes what the Kural says in two couplets (1122, 1124).

colophon.thurai: போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man leaving for work, torn by the parting

comparisons.tenor: the water rushing in the wheel ruts
the pulse pods splitting open

comparisons.vehicle: இருதலைக் கொள்ளி இடைநின்று வருந்தி ஒருதலைப் படாஅ உறவி
comparisons.tenor: the man torn between duty and love
her bond with him
her love
parting from her

occasion.words: போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

340.reading: As evening falls after a day meeting in the punnai shade, the friend asks the lover to give up leaving, since the tide has filled the backwaters, snakes and fierce fish crowd the path and the girl, lovely as Thiraiyan's Pavaththiri, is fading, and to stay the night in their fishing village, where they will feed him rice and curd porridge bought with fresh fish and anoint him with sandal paste, where the shark-torn nets hang idle on the screwpine.
340.nuance: Fed and anointed as a guest, the lover would be received openly by her people: the invitation to stay is the friend's push toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai grove, fishermen and sharks

comparisons.tenor: the girl's fresh beauty

links.note: 326 likens the young woman's unerring eyes to the spear raised by Pazhaiyan, lord of Por and the Cholas' champion; 44 recalls the battle in which Pazhaiyan fell (பழையன் பட்டென) and Chenni avenged him.
links.teaches: Akam poets drew on both halves of one champion's story, his unfailing aim for a woman's dangerous eyes and his death for the scale of a war that keeps a husband from home, so the hero's fame served love poetry whole.

links.note: Both are marutham speeches by a courtesan meant for the hearing of others, and both stake her bangles on Chola martial formulas: 186 says the lord never broke her bangles, using Pazhaiyan's 'rain of arrows, cloud-dark shields' (மாரி அம்பின் மழைத்தோல்); 336 applies the same phrase to the Cholas and curses her bangles to break like the Aryans at Vallam.
links.teaches: The pair shows the courtesan's boast as a set form: her bangles stand for her hold on the man, and she guarantees them with the same Chola war formula, as a warrior swears by his king.

links.note: 338 wishes love to last like the Porai's Kolli; 209 tells how Kari killed Ori and gave Kolli to the Cheras, who set a goddess image there.
links.teaches: Read with 209, the hero's figure of permanence is a hill that changed lords by a killing, so what the poet makes lasting is the hill itself, not any house that held it.

links.note: Purananuru 158 names Kolli as the hill Ori ruled, among seven givers now dead; Akananuru 338 calls Kolli the Porai's and makes it the measure of a love that must not perish.
links.teaches: The puram poem remembers Kolli by a dead patron and the akam poem by its new Chera master, so the hill a lover swears by already carries the record of a fallen lord.

links.note: Both name Thithiyan as lord of Pothiyil: 25 has his drums echoed in the waterfalls of the hills the absent man crossed; 322 makes his guarded, honey-hung peak the measure of how hard the girl is to reach.
links.teaches: One chief's hill serves two opposite uses, the distance a husband has gone and the closeness a lover cannot reach, which shows akam poets taking a puram place for its fit to the speaker's situation, not for its praise.

links.note: Both poems in this chapter name Thithiyan: 322 his war elephants and his guarded Pothiyil; 331 his daily court, his gifts to bards and the sword he drew against the Velir.
links.teaches: The same patron lends the frustrated lover his inaccessible hill and the abandoned wife his sword, so each speaker takes from a king's fame the face that matches her or his own trouble.

links.note: 85 names Thiraiyan's Venkatam hill on the road the husband crossed; 340 names Thiraiyan's flowery seaside town Pavaththiri as the measure of the girl's beauty.
links.teaches: The same chief furnishes a mountain for a paalai poem and a shore town for a neythal one, so a patron's domain was divided among the landscapes as the thinai required.

links.note: Same thurai: a man, his task done, urges his charioteer home. 34 drives by the stag that feeds and guards its doe; 334 by the breaking rains, hail and peacocks, and by the tribute won with the war drum.
links.teaches: Together they show the homecoming poem built in two ways: by a creature whose care mirrors the husband's intent (34), or by the season itself whose arrival is the pledge kept (334).

links.note: Both are night-tryst poems the lover overhears, and both close on the same formula, a tusker and his mate asleep on the plantain slope (வாழையஞ் சிலம்பிற் றுஞ்சும் / வாழையம் சிலம்பில் துஞ்சும்): in 328 he strokes a mate who has just calved, in 332 he lies down with her after killing a tiger.
links.teaches: A shared formula takes a different act each time to suit the speech: the calving mate presses toward married life in a poem of fear, the tiger-killing protector confirms the lover in a poem of praise.

links.note: Both are men arguing with hearts set on wealth, and both make the desert's killers the argument: in 327 the archers pity no victim and grieve only when they miss; in 337 the Mazhavar kill a starving messenger in case he has gold and leave scorning his rags.
links.teaches: Side by side they show the road weighing a man's life only by what he might carry, which is the very reckoning the heart is making when it trades her company for wealth.

links.note: Kural 1124: she is living to my life when with me and dying when she leaves; Akananuru 339 ends with love like the life's living and parting like dying, spoken by a husband as he sets out.
links.teaches: The Kural says it in courtship as praise; the poem puts the same claim in the mouth of a man choosing to leave, so the saying becomes the cost he knowingly pays, burning at both ends of the firebrand.

links.note: Kural 1122 calls the bond with the girl that of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை ... நட்பு); 339 has the same word and image, friendship like life joined to the body (யாக்கைக்கு உயிர்இயைந் தன்ன நட்பின்).
links.teaches: The shared image and even the shared word நட்பு show the Kural's couplet as a distilled form of an akam figure that the poem still spends a scene of departure to earn.

links.note: Kural 247 grants that this world is not for those without wealth; Akananuru 335 opens by conceding that even the most compassionate cannot give without wealth, then gives up the journey for wealth anyway.
links.teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's premise about wealth in so many words yet refuses its practical pull, showing that the premise alone did not settle whether a husband should leave home to earn.

links.note: Kural 629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not feel the pain within pain; Akananuru 327 tells the heart that joy and grief come by turns like day and night, so it need not go seeking hardship for wealth.
links.teaches: The same doctrine of joy and grief in turn, which the Kural uses to teach calm under misfortune, becomes in the lover's mouth an argument for staying home rather than chasing gain.

links.note: Kural 81: all of keeping house is for receiving guests; in Akananuru 324 the attendants announce the husband's return by saying his wife will now have guests to feed too.
links.teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule from the inside of an absence: hospitality belonged to the couple, so a wife alone could not host, and the husband's return is announced as the return of guests.

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place and time of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons of 322, 328, 332, 338 and 340 (அல்லகுறி, இரவுக்குறி, பகற் குறி)

new_concepts.gloss: marriage as the end of secret love, which the friend or the heroine presses the lover toward
new_concepts.label_source: ours: the tradition's term; 328 and 340 imply it without naming it

source_issues: 325, 327, 328, 332: the colophon thurai carries a stray footnote numeral (1கொண்டு, 2நெஞ்சினை, 1தலைமகள்); 325's (1) has no second alternative.
331 line 8: பிறக் கெரழிய looks like a misprint for பிறக்கு ஒழிய (the vowel sign ொ split into ெ and ர).
335 line 7: மராஅத்துக் பொளிபிளந்து has க் before ப, an irregular sandhi; probably a misprint for மராஅத்துப் பொளி.
337: the colophon thurai names the speaker தலைமகள், but the one who went for wealth, came back and speaks to his heart is the man; read தலைமகன்.
332 line 12: the text flag records a repaired stray space before a dead consonant.
325, 327, 333, 337: opening single quotation marks at the start of the speech are never closed.
